## Activity 1 · The AI's t-test {#act1 .activity}

[Pairs · 10 minutes · Lab 06, Step 4]{.act-label}

```{=html}
<pre class="code-slide"><span>before = df.loc[df.period == "before", "C6H6_ugm3"].dropna()</span><span>after = df.loc[df.period == "after", "C6H6_ugm3"].dropna()</span><span>t, p = stats.ttest_ind(after, before, equal_var=False)</span><span>print(f"n = {len(before) + len(after)}, p = {p:.1e}")</span><span><b class="c"># "p &lt; 0.05: the traffic plan changed benzene."</b></span></pre>
```

::: {.prompt .small}
The code runs and p is computed correctly for what it was given. Which assumption of the t-test does this data break, and what does that do to p?
:::

::: {.selfstudy}
Studying alone: write your answer, then go on.
:::

## What to change {#act1-fix}

::: {.beforeafter}
::: {}
[The assumption]{.label}
The t-test treats 667 hours as 667 independent measurements. Neighboring hours correlate at 0.84, and every day repeats its rush hours. The standard error is too small, so p is too small: for Demo A, 0.00006.
:::
::: {}
[A first fix]{.label}
One value per day: 14 against 14. For Demo A, p becomes 0.13 and the 95 % confidence interval widens from 1.6 to 4.5 µg/m³. The comment's "changed" also claims a cause that no test checked.
:::
:::

[Count what is independent before you count values.]{.note-line}

      g += `<circle cx="${X(d)}" cy="${V(y)}" r="9" fill="#E29A2D" stroke="#1C242B" stroke-width="2"/><text x="${X(d) + 14}" y="${V(y) + 6}" font-size="18" font-weight="700" fill="#1C242B">${t}</text>`;
      for (const s of [1, -1]) g += `<line x1="${L}" x2="${W - R}" y1="${V(s * Math.abs(y))}" y2="${V(s * Math.abs(y))}" stroke="#66727C" stroke-dasharray="5 5" opacity=".6"/>`;
    });

      demo: 'Demo A (−1.69): 45 % of ordinary dates show a difference at least this large. Demo B (−5.93): only 1 of 306 does. Only Demo B stands out from an ordinary fortnight.',
    }[v];
    root.querySelectorAll('[data-v]').forEach((b) => b.setAttribute('aria-pressed', b.dataset.v === v));
  }
  root.querySelectorAll('[data-v]').forEach((b) => b.addEventListener('click', () => draw(b.dataset.v)));

[Lab 06, Step 7: 306 dates, 14 days each side. Data: De Vito, UCI Air Quality, doi:10.24432/C59K5F, CC BY 4.0.]{.source}

## Why the tests fire too often {#why}

::: {.checks3}
::: {.c4}
[Hours are not independent]{.label}
Neighboring hours correlate at 0.84 and the daily cycle repeats. 667 hours carry far less information than 667 values.
:::
::: {.c4}
[Days are not either]{.label}
Neighboring days correlate at 0.6: weather lasts several days. 14 days count as fewer than 14.
:::
::: {.c4}
[Fortnights differ]{.label}
Season and holidays move the level. The t-test sees only the scatter inside each fortnight, not how much ordinary fortnights differ.
:::
:::

[Placebo dates measure the third point directly: they are the year's own record of "nothing changed".]{.note-line}

## What you can claim {#claim}

::: {.beforeafter}
::: {}
[Demo A · 29 July 2004]{.label}
−1.7 µg/m³ (95 % confidence interval −3.9 to 0.5), p = 0.13 on daily means. 45 % of ordinary dates show a difference this large. The data do not show an effect.
:::
::: {}
[Demo B · 7 November 2004]{.label}
−5.9 µg/m³ (−8.9 to −3.0), p = 0.0004. Only 1 of 306 ordinary dates shows a difference this large. A real shift, but the data cannot say whether the traffic plan or the November weather caused it.
:::
:::

[Before a decision, ask for a comparison that rules out the other cause: a station the plan did not touch, or the same weeks in another year.]{.note-line}

## Activity 2 · Lab 06, Steps 4 to 10 {#act2 .activity}

[Individual · 25 minutes · laptop or phone]{.act-label}

1. Open **Lab 06**. Press **Open a saved study** if you saved one in Session 11.
2. Step 4: write your answer before you compare.
